```{r}

#| include: false

Sys.setenv(TZ = "UTC")

knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
data_dir <- normalizePath(file.path(dirname(knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE)),
                                    "../../dev/article-data/plot-sampling"))
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = data_dir)
```

A stand table describes how trees are distributed among species and diameter
classes, usually in trees per hectare. We estimate a forest stand table by
combining a magnitude model for overall tree density, a composition model
for species, and a conditional composition model for diameter at breast
height (DBH) within each species. Using the
[shared simulated forest](plot-sampling-data.html), we fit all three
components, examine parameter estimates and fitted values, and compare
predicted forest species-by-DBH densities with truth.

The [magnitude article](magnitude-plot-sampling.html) and
[composition article](composition-plot-sampling.html) explain the individual
components. The [DBH article](dbh-plot-sampling.html) combines magnitude and
DBH allocation after summing over species. Here we retain species information and add
a second allocation within each species to describe its DBH distribution.
The magnitude model predicts total
counts at new locations, and the composition models allocate them among
species and then DBH classes. We therefore do not need to supply known
prediction-cell totals.

::: {.alert .alert-info role="note"}
**Example data**

[Download the plot-sampling data (ZIP)](downloads/plot-sampling.zip){.btn .btn-primary download="plot-sampling.zip"}

The introductory plot-sampling articles use this same archive.
Extract it and use the folder containing `data/` as your R working directory.
:::

## Read the data

The shared data contain 151 sampled plots and 4,812 prediction cells, with
simulated counts for pine, oak, and birch in five DBH classes. Each class
includes its lower bound and excludes its upper bound; `50+` includes trees
at least 50 cm in diameter. The predictor `x` is p95 canopy height standardized
using the plots' mean and standard deviation.

We read the plot and prediction tables, then arrange the plot counts into
one row per plot, species, and DBH class. Zero counts remain in the table.

```{r}
#| label: read-data

library(magComp)
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(1)

plots <- read_csv("data/plots.csv")

prediction <- read_csv("data/prediction.csv")

species_order <- c("pine", "oak", "birch")
dbh_classes <- c("10-20", "20-30", "30-40", "40-50", "50+")

trees <- plots |>
  select(plot_id, area, x, contains(":")) |>
  pivot_longer(contains(":"), names_to = c("species", "dbh_class"),
               names_sep = ":", values_to = "count") |>
  mutate(
    species = factor(species, levels = species_order),
    dbh_class = ordered(dbh_class, levels = dbh_classes)
  ) |>
  arrange(plot_id, species, dbh_class)

trees |>
  filter(plot_id == 1) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Each plot has 15 species-by-DBH counts. Their sum gives its total tree count;
summing within species gives the species totals.

## How the model components fit together

For plot $i$, let $N_i$ be its total tree count, $a_i$ its sampled area in
hectares, and $M_i$ its expected density in trees/ha. The magnitude model is

$$
\log M_i=\beta_0+\beta_1 x_i,\qquad
N_i\mid M_i,r_M\sim\operatorname{NB}(a_i M_i,r_M),
$$

where the negative-binomial distribution has mean $a_i M_i$ and size $r_M$.
The generating values are $\beta_0=\log(350)$, $\beta_1=-0.2$, and $r_M=50$.
Thus, expected density at average plot p95 is 350 trees/ha.

Let $A$ denote species and $B$ denote DBH class. Write $q_{ia}$ for the
probability of species $a$ and $r_{ib\mid a}$ for the probability of DBH
class $b$ within that species. The species probabilities denoted $p_{ij}$
in the composition article are now $q_{ia}$; we use $p_{iab}$ for the joint
species-by-DBH probability,

$$
p_{iab}=q_{ia}\,r_{ib\mid a}.
$$

Species probabilities sum to one, and DBH probabilities sum to one within
each species. The 15 joint probabilities therefore sum to one. Conditional
on $N_i$, the counts follow a multinomial distribution with those
probabilities. For species $a$ and DBH class $b$, expected density is
$M_i p_{iab}$ and expected plot count is $a_i M_i p_{iab}$.

Both composition components use sequential probit allocation. Trees are
allocated to pine, then oak, with birch receiving the remainder. Within each
species, allocation proceeds through the DBH classes from smallest to
largest. Each allocation step has its own intercept and canopy-height
slope, with `pnorm()` converting their linear expression to a conditional
probability. The last DBH class receives the remaining trees of that species.

The species and DBH models have separate regression coefficients, denoted
by $\alpha$. Each species has its own set of DBH coefficients. We use the
same predictor `x` in all components; the formulas also allow different
predictors for magnitude, species, and conditional DBH composition.

## Fit the full model

We supply the category columns in species-then-DBH order.
`species ~ x` specifies species allocation, and `dbh_class | species ~ x`
specifies DBH allocation within each species.

```{r}
#| label: fit

dat <- magCompData(
  trees,
  unit = plot_id, categories = c(species, dbh_class),
  tree_count = count, design = fixedArea(area)
)

fit <- magComp(
  dat,
  magnitude = ~ x,
  composition = magCompComposition(
    species ~ x,
    dbh_class | species ~ x
  ),
  control = magCompControl(
    n_samples = 2000,
    n_burn = 1000,
    n_chains = 3,
    n_cores = 3,
    chain_seeds = 1:3,
    verbose = FALSE
  )
)
```

The factor levels specify the allocation sequences. Ordering the DBH factor
does not by itself smooth coefficients across classes; this example uses
independent Normal coefficient priors. Negative-binomial size is estimated
under its default Gamma prior with shape 1 and rate 0.01. We retain the
automatic starting values.

Each of three MCMC chains runs for 2,000 iterations and discards the first
1,000. We use all 3,000 retained draws for parameter summaries.

### Magnitude and species parameters

We use `summary()` to obtain posterior estimates, 95% credible intervals,
and chain diagnostics, then add the generating values from the data article.

```{r}
#| label: main-parameters

parameter_summary <- summary(fit)

# Magnitude rows are the intercept, canopy-height slope, and size.
magnitude_summary <- parameter_summary |>
  filter(component == "magnitude") |>
  mutate(truth = c(log(350), -0.2, 50))

true_alpha <- c("pine:(Intercept)" = 0, "pine:x" = 0.5,
                "oak:(Intercept)" = -0.5, "oak:x" = -0.5)

species_summary <- parameter_summary |>
  filter(block == "species") |>
  mutate(truth = true_alpha[index])

bind_rows(magnitude_summary, species_summary) |>
  select(symbol, truth, mean, q2_5, q97_5, rhat, ess) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    col.names = c("Parameter", "Truth", "Mean", "2.5%", "97.5%", "R-hat", "ESS")
  )
```

`beta[0]` is log expected density at average plot p95, and `beta[x]` is its
change for a one-standard-deviation increase in p95. Exponentiating the
slope gives the corresponding multiplier on density. The species `alpha`
coefficients describe conditional probit probabilities, as in the
composition article. R-hat values near one indicate agreement among chains;
ESS is the effective sample size after accounting for dependence among draws.

### DBH allocation coefficients

There are 24 DBH coefficients, an intercept and slope for each of four
allocation steps within each of three species. We arrange their generating
values as a table and match them to the fitted parameter labels.

```{r}
#| label: dbh-parameters

true_dbh <- tibble(
  species = rep(species_order, each = 4),
  dbh_class = rep(dbh_classes[1:4], times = 3),
  intercept = c(-1, -0.5, 0, 0.5,
                -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1,
                 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5),
  slope = c(-0.4, -0.3, -0.2, -0.1,
            -0.3, -0.3, -0.2, -0.2,
            -0.2, -0.2, -0.1, -0.1)
) |>
  pivot_longer(c(intercept, slope), names_to = "coefficient",
               values_to = "truth") |>
  mutate(index = paste(species, dbh_class,
                        if_else(coefficient == "intercept", "(Intercept)", "x"),
                        sep = ":"))

dbh_summary <- parameter_summary |>
  filter(block == "dbh_class|species") |>
  left_join(true_dbh, by = "index") |>
  mutate(
    species = factor(species, levels = species_order),
    dbh_class = ordered(dbh_class, levels = dbh_classes[1:4]),
    coefficient = factor(coefficient, levels = c("intercept", "slope"),
                          labels = c("Intercept", "Canopy-height slope"))
  )
```

We compare the estimated coefficients and intervals with truth. A DBH
slope describes allocation to that class among the trees of the species
still available after earlier classes.

```{r}
#| label: fig-dbh-parameters
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| fig-cap: "DBH allocation coefficients by species. Blue points and bars show posterior means and 95% credible intervals; black horizontal marks show generating values. The final DBH class receives the remainder and has no separate coefficient."

ggplot(dbh_summary, aes(dbh_class, mean)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = q2_5, ymax = q97_5), width = 0.15,
                color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2", size = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(y = truth), shape = 95, size = 6) +
  facet_grid(coefficient ~ species, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "DBH class (cm)", y = "Coefficient") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The later birch allocation steps have wider intervals because relatively
few birch trees remain to inform those coefficients.

Across the `r nrow(parameter_summary)` parameters, the largest R-hat is
`r round(max(parameter_summary$rhat), 3)` and the smallest ESS is about
`r round(min(parameter_summary$ess))`. Trace plots are available with
`plot(fit)` when examining individual chains.

## Examine fitted values

For a full model, `fitted(fit)` returns posterior means for overall density,
joint category probabilities, category densities, and category counts.
Here we request category densities and arrange the first plot's fitted
values as a stand table.

```{r}
#| label: fitted-values

fitted_mean <- fitted(fit, type = "density")

# Category columns follow DBH class within species.
first_plot <- matrix(
  fitted_mean$density[1, ], nrow = length(dbh_classes),
  dimnames = list(dbh_classes, species_order)
)

knitr::kable(first_plot, digits = 1)
```

Entries are fitted densities in trees/ha. Their sum is the fitted overall
density for that plot. These are expected densities under the fitted model;
the observed counts divided by plot area fluctuate around them.

## Predict and aggregate across the forest

For each selected posterior draw, prediction first generates a total count
from the negative-binomial model at each cell. It then allocates the count
among species and DBH classes. `type = "density"` returns those counts
divided by cell area. We supply only IDs, canopy height, and cell areas;
the simulated cell counts are reserved for comparison with truth.

```{r}
#| label: predict

predictions <- predict(
  fit,
  prediction |> select(plot_id, x, area),
  type = "density",
  target = "observation",
  n_draws = 100,
  summary = "samples"
)

# Prediction cell x species-by-DBH category x retained draw x chain.
dim(predictions$density)
```

The array contains 4,812 cells, 15 categories, 100 retained draws, and three
chains. These draws include parameter uncertainty and variation in both
total counts and their allocation.

We use `standSummary()` to average densities across the forest within each
draw, weighting by cell area. Smaller boundary cells contribute less to
the forest average. Omitting `group` produces a forest-wide summary.

```{r}
#| label: forest-estimates

forest_predictions <- standSummary(
  predictions,
  data = prediction,
  unit = plot_id,
  represented_area = area,
  summary = "samples"
)

forest_summary <- summary(forest_predictions)

forest_estimates <- forest_summary |>
  as_tibble() |>
  separate_wider_delim(category, delim = ":", names = c("species", "dbh_class")) |>
  mutate(
    species = factor(species, levels = species_order),
    dbh_class = ordered(dbh_class, levels = dbh_classes)
  )

forest_estimates |>
  select(dbh_class, species, mean) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = species, values_from = mean) |>
  arrange(dbh_class) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

This is the estimated forest stand table in trees/ha. Each entry is a
posterior predictive mean. We calculate intervals from the aggregated
draws, including both count variation and parameter uncertainty.

## Compare species-by-DBH distributions with truth

The true forest density for each species-by-DBH category is its simulated
count summed over prediction cells, divided by their combined area. This
is the same area-weighted density calculation used for predictions.

```{r}
#| label: forest-truth

forest_truth <- prediction |>
  select(contains(":")) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("species", "dbh_class"),
               names_sep = ":", values_to = "count") |>
  group_by(species, dbh_class) |>
  summarise(truth = sum(count) / sum(prediction$area), .groups = "drop")

comparison <- forest_estimates |>
  left_join(forest_truth, by = c("species", "dbh_class")) |>
  mutate(
    species = factor(species, levels = species_order),
    dbh_class = ordered(dbh_class, levels = dbh_classes)
  )
```

We plot each species' DBH distribution using separate estimates for the
diameter classes. Black horizontal marks show the realized forest densities
from the simulated population.

```{r}
#| label: fig-forest-distributions
#| fig-cap: "Forest species-by-DBH densities. Blue points and bars show posterior predictive means and 95% intervals; black horizontal marks show simulated truth."

ggplot(comparison, aes(dbh_class, mean)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = q2_5, ymax = q97_5), width = 0.15,
                color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(aes(shape = "Estimate"), color = "#0072B2", size = 2.5) +
  geom_point(aes(y = truth, shape = "Truth"), size = 6) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Truth" = 95, "Estimate" = 16),
                     breaks = c("Truth", "Estimate"), name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~ species, nrow = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = "DBH class (cm)", y = "Trees per hectare") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The estimates follow the main features of the simulated distributions.
Pine is most abundant in the middle DBH classes, while oak and birch are
concentrated in the smaller classes. The intervals describe uncertainty in
the forest's species-by-DBH densities, including uncertainty about total
abundance. Within each draw, species and DBH allocations sum to that draw's
overall density.

The same predictions can produce stand tables by supplying the
cell–stand area table to `standSummary()` with `group = stand_id`, as in the
magnitude article. Summaries by species or DBH class are obtained by adding
the relevant category densities within each draw before calculating intervals.

The next article adds [stratum-specific intercepts](stratum-effects-plot-sampling.html)
to describe differences among groups of stands; its
[companion](stratum-slopes-plot-sampling.html) also allows canopy-height slopes
to vary. Later articles introduce [spatial effects](spatial-effects-plot-sampling.html),
[effects in within-species DBH allocation](conditional-dbh-effects-plot-sampling.html),
and [space-time effects](space-time-effects-plot-sampling.html).
Each extension uses its own simulated population in the same forest.
